data.title: Middle East Eye: Diplomats from 18 Muslim-majority countries condemn Israeli strike on Nasser hospital
data.author: Areeb Ullah
data.summary:
Diplomats from 18 Muslim-majority countries condemn Israeli strike on Nasser hospital
Top diplomats from 18 Muslim-majority countries strongly condemned an Israeli strike on the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis.
Countries that condemned the strike include Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan.
The attack left at least six people dead, including a child and a surgeon, prompting accusations from ministers that Israel is violating international humanitarian law.
In the joint declaration, the foreign ministers condemned ongoing assaults against Palestinians, warning that violence threatens to collapse the ceasefire in Gaza.
The countries accused Israel of blockading critical humanitarian assistance- specifically medical shipments and winter supplies-which they warned leaves infants and children exposed to failing water, sanitation, and healthcare systems as winter sets in.
Pressing for immediate compliance, the coalition called on Israel to strictly enforce the truce, facilitate unhindered aid deliveries, and fully honour its obligations under the ceasefire framework.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Three Israelis emerge as possible successors to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, local media says
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Three Israelis emerge as possible successors to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, local media says
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Sat, 11/14/2026 - 11:36
Michael Kagan, Eyal Waldman and Johny Srouji are among the names being discussed after Huang’s immediate departure
Greenpeace activists hold a banner protesting against Nvidia’s environmental impact as chief executive Jensen Huang delivers a keynote speech at the GTC Berlin AI conference on 21 October 2026 (John MacDougall/AFP)
Off
Three Israeli technology executives have emerged among the possible successors to Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after leading the artificial intelligence chipmaker for more than three decades.
Huang’s departure, announced on 12 November, took effect immediately. Nvidia’s board appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while it searches for a permanent successor.
The company said it would consider both internal and external candidates.
Israeli media have named Michael Kagan, Nvidia’s chief technology officer; Eyal Waldman, co-founder and former chief executive of Israeli networking company Mellanox; and Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, as possible contenders.
Kagan co-founded Mellanox in 1999 and joined Nvidia after it acquired the company in 2020 for about $6.9bn.
He has since served as Nvidia’s chief technology officer, focusing on technologies that allow thousands of processors to communicate within large data centres.
Waldman also co-founded Mellanox and served as its chief executive before the acquisition. Unlike Kagan, he is no longer part of Nvidia’s management.
Ynet has also reported that he is in the succession discussions.
Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, is one of the key figures behind the company’s in-house chip development.
He joined Apple in 2008 and led the development of processors used in its products, including those underpinning its transition from Intel processors to Apple Silicon.

US Marines and sailors prepare F-35B fighter jets for flight operations aboard the USS Essex in the US Fifth Fleet’s area of operations on 27 September 2018 (AFP)

The US Navy has fired several top officers without its customary public announcements, drawing criticism from lawmakers amid heightened security concerns at American military installations and tensions with Iran.
Those removed include the leadership team of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota. Its commander, second-in-command and senior enlisted sailor were relieved of their duties in October after the submarine reportedly struck something on the seabed.
The Navy also sacked Commander Caitlin Cunningham from her position leading the USS Michael Murphy destroyer on 27 September, citing a “loss of confidence”, according to a defence official.
The vessel had been deployed to support operations against Iran.
Admiral Brian Monahan, who served as attending physician to Congress and the Supreme Court for nearly 18 years, is also reported to have left his post amid an investigation.
Democratic Representatives Joe Courtney and Adam Smith said the Navy had failed to notify the House Armed Services Committee.
In a letter to acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and the service’s top uniformed officer, Admiral Daryl Caudle, they expressed “deep frustration” over the lack of communication.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Saudi Arabia executes former child protester Jawad Qureiris
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Saudi Arabia executes former child protester Jawad Qureiris
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Sat, 11/14/2026 - 16:32
Rights groups condemn secret execution of former child protester as a tool of political oppression under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman
This picture shows a poster depicting King Salman bin Abdulaziz (R), and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (L) in Riyadh on May 12, 2025 (AFP)
Off
Saudi Arabia executed a man who was detained as a child, alongside another Saudi national from the Kingdom’s Shia-majority Eastern Province.
In a statement on Saturday, the Saudi Press Agency confirmed that Riyadh had executed Jawad Qureiris.
Hailing from a prominent Shia-majority family in the Kingdom’s Eastern Province, Qureiris was a former child defendant who was just 14 to 15 years old during the 2011-12 Arab Spring protests.
Qureiris’ family has a documented history of encounters with state security: one of his brothers was killed by security forces, while another was arrested at age 13 and faced capital charges related to alleged offences committed when he was nine years old.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Interior also announced that Fadel bin Hassan bin Abdullah Al-Safwani was executed on Saturday.
The ministry claimed the men were convicted of “terrorist crimes,” alleging they joined a foreign terrorist organisation, opened fire on security personnel and vehicles with weapons and explosives, possessed live ammunition, and provided logistical and financial support for operations within the Kingdom.
According to the SPA statement, the cases passed through specialised criminal courts, where the men’s legal responsibility was established before the verdicts were upheld by the Supreme Court and ratified via a royal decree.
Qureiris was arrested in December 2020 and charged with offences related to taking part in protests and organising on social media.

US Senator John Fetterman speaks to reporters at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on January 9, 2025. (Allison Robbert/AFP)

Democratic Senator John Fetterman suggested on Saturday that he could leave his party if Senate Democrats chose a leader he considered insufficiently pro-Israel.
Fetterman singled out Senator Chris Van Hollen, a critic of Israel who on Thursday challenged Chuck Schumer, the septuagenarian hardline pro-Israel Democrat, for the Senate leadership. Van Hollen said the party needed new leadership after voters opted for change in this month’s midterm elections.
“Yeah, absolutely,” Fetterman said in a Fox News interview on Saturday when asked whether he had a red line that would make him “walk away” from the party.
“It would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being very anti, hostile to Israel,” said Fetterman, who has backed the Israeli genocide and ethnic cleansing in Gaza.
Democrats won 55 Senate seats in the midterms, giving them a comfortable majority. There had been speculation that Fetterman could defect to the Republicans if Democrats won just 51 seats, as many expected. With 55 seats, the party can retain its majority without him.
The Pennsylvania senator said he had yet to decide what he would do if Van Hollen became majority leader.
After visiting the Gaza border in September 2025, Van Hollen said: “In Gaza, the Netanyahu government is implementing its goal through the near-total destruction of civilian infrastructure and its use of food as a weapon of war.”

data.title: Middle East Eye: Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis killed in Israeli strike on Khan Younis
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis killed in Israeli strike on Khan Younis
Hamas' armed wing said on Sunday that a senior commander who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel had been killed in an Israeli airstrike.
The Al-Qassam Brigades identified the commander as Samir Abu Younis, 53, the commander of its Rafah brigade, and said he was killed on Saturday.
The Israeli military said on Sunday it had struck a senior commander in Hamas' armed wing but did not identify him.
Medics said Abu Younis was killed and others were wounded in an airstrike that targeted him in a street in the Mawasi area of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip.
Hamas said Abu Younis joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and had held several senior operational roles in Rafah before becoming commander of the brigade.
Hamas said his funeral would be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis.
An October ​2025 ceasefire halted major fighting but has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas' disarmament.
Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed ​during the same period.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel's military campaign against Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Eisenkot calls Netanyahu's unity government call 'yet another spin move'
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Eisenkot calls Netanyahu's unity government call 'yet another spin move'
Israeli opposition leader and prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot has accused Benjamin Netanyahu of resorting to political tricks to delay the formation of a new government, saying his latest call for negotiations was "yet another spin move".
In a post on X, Eisenkot said Netanyahu knew that a meeting between the negotiating teams of Likud and Yesh Atid had already been scheduled for Monday.
"This is the latest bluff: Netanyahu calls for negotiations after they have already been scheduled, claims he wants unity, but disgraces a state ceremony in the Knesset and divides and incites as if there were no tomorrow," Eisenkot wrote.
The remarks come after an inconclusive election left the Knesset without a clear governing majority, with rival political camps seeking to assemble the numbers needed to form the next government.
Eisenkot said Netanyahu knew he had lost the election and that there was "an overwhelming majority against him among the citizens of Israel and in the Knesset".
He accused the outgoing prime minister of mounting "a delaying action" to make it difficult to form a new government and prevent the replacement of the Knesset speaker.
Eisenkot reiterated that the conditions for joining an emergency government under his leadership included acceptance of the principles he had outlined and "a break with the extremists".

Saudi-led coalition intercepts third drone as Houthis claim downing aircraft
Saudi-led coalition forces have shot down yet another Houthi drone in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region, according to Colonel Turki al-Malki, spokesman for the coalition.
It’s the third drone the coalition says it has shot down over the region in the last three hours, along with two ballistic missiles that were headed for Riyadh.
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X that they have shot down a Saudi Arabian armed reconnaissance aircraft in the airspace of al-Jawf.
Saree said this is the fifth aircraft the Houthis have shot down since the escalation began.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel.
But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.
He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war.
"I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly," Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday.
Trump's private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming.
CALLS WITH SAUDI ARABIA AND TURKEY
In phone calls over the past two weeks, Trump asked for opinions from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who both urged him not to resume attacks on Iran, according to a senior US official and another person familiar with the matter. They said Trump made no commitment either way.
Trump told bin Salman on 31 October that he was planning to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for him to hold off, arguing that economic sanctions against Iran were working, according to two more people familiar with the discussion.
Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
